stories.body:
I felt a duty to write about the Tang dynasty and its incredible social and cultural sophistication – but also to connect my Chinese past with my child

Tang

During the Tang dynasty , which lasted from the seventh to the early 10th century, Vikings were raiding the coasts of what today is called Europe. In the small archipelago now known as Britain, Anglo-Saxon kingdoms flitted by. Meanwhile, in Mesoamerica, after 3,000 years of flourishing, the Maya civilisation was collapsing . In the east, China had been united for nine centuries and the Tang dynasty was already a proverbial high point of world culture.

The Tang dynasty achieved an incredible level of social and cultural sophistication. Advances in science and medicine, sublime poetry, mystical paintings, high fashion in women’s clothing beyond the palace walls, exquisite ceramic and pottery arts, the invention of gunpowder and printing, highly elaborate cuisine, creative urban design and much more. It was a truly cosmopolitan empire with dynamic diplomatic relations with the neighbouring kingdoms.

When I ponder this, an urge arises in me: a kind of duty, if you like, to write about this era. The Tang contrasts sharply with the image of a self-enclosed, inward-looking China , one that the west has long liked to promote. An open, cosmopolitan melting pot, it was the eastern centre into which flowed the riches of the silk roads that stretched all the way to the Byzantine empire.

But still, why the Tang? And why learn about the Tang from me? I have my own story to tell, which has no pretence to objectivity. My story involves a specific, passionate reconnection with my own heritage. I wanted to return to China after a long absence. The last time I was there had been a decade before, along with my then three-month-old child, Moon. My desire to go back was in part for her, now 11 years old. So she and I set off on a journey back to the cultural womb from which I had emerged and had left behind. I had to explain the Chinese past not only to the child, but to myself.

Xi’an

Our journey began in Xi’an, the capital of the Tang dynasty . A high-speed train had brought us from Beijing on a searingly hot day in July. On the road, the tarmac glistened and oozed out its black heat, while the city roared in full force with an immense river of traffic.

I had booked a traditional-looking hotel, thinking we should taste more of the old China. When we reached the hotel, we had to squeeze ourselves in between a gang of businessmen all wearing black suits with alcohol-flushed faces. They spoke at high volume, while coughing and hawking. Was it a gathering for people with respiratory illnesses? I could smell their strong cigarettes from several metres away. With “no smoking” signs in the lobby, they stood by the hotel gate puffing away while cracking loud jokes. They spoke Shanxi dialect and I could vaguely make out that their laughter was to do with food and women. How familiar all this was; men in suits, chain-smoking, looking for girls – the kind of stuff that came with the recent wealth from the “Chinese miracle”. Where were the women, though? As usual, women worked. The receptionist and the manager were women. They gave us the room key after taking our money.

Our room reeked of smoke; even the white bedding. We wanted to venture out immediately. We jumped into an air-conditioned taxi and set off to find some famous landmarks.

An hour later we were standing by the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda . Moon hid under a nearby pomegranate tree, sucking an ice lolly, her chestnut-coloured hair tangled with sweat. Beyond the deafening sound of cicadas high up in the tree, the heat formed a shimmering layer of pink fog above the pagoda. Sweat was dripping from my eyebrows, obscuring my vision.

Everyone in China knows that Xi’an is one of the oldest cities in the country. It’s our Rome or Athens. Over a 2,000-year period, it served as the capital for several dynasties, though it was called Chang’an back then. Traces of the Tang are everywhere. Like many other old monuments, the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda of today is not original. Built at the beginning of the Tang in the seventh century, it was restored in the eighth century, then rebuilt in the 16th century after an earthquake. Constructed of brick and wood, the facade displays elaborate sculptures and carvings on the eaves. We joined a swirl of tourists around the tall tower, but we were not allowed to enter because it is too fragile for crowds.

Moon was born and brought up in England. She had never experienced this climate, nor such crowds massed around her. There was not a single puff of wind. I feared she might get sunstroke. Hopping from the shadow of one tree to another, we managed to exit the park.

Once outside, we leaned on the ancient city walls, enjoying the small respite offered by the shade. The wall, I read, was 14km in length, mainly built in the Ming dynasty in the 14th century. But the original was Tang. Xi’an is a great palimpsest on which many cultures have written their lives. This is very different from Rome or Athens, which are full of original ruins. Nothing in China can remain as ruins – the government either recreates the supposed original or builds something totally new. Ruins cannot exist under communism.

Numbers

We wandered around a street market looking at all kinds of Chinese vegetables. We were eating stir-fried potato strips with vinegar and chilli.

‘What’s this, Mum?’ Moon prodded a plate of white vegetables with her chopsticks.

‘They are lotus root slices. Try it!’

Embarking on this trip led me to think about my own relationship to China, but also about my daughter’s. Such an immense past. I wondered how I could educate her. What importance could it hold for her? Moon was English, or British: her first language was English, despite my ongoing efforts to fill her ears with my native tongue. These efforts have resulted only in the most moderate success. Moon could understand my Chinese, but it was as though the language had not penetrated beneath her skin. In England, at the end of a school day, she would say to me: “I find history difficult to enjoy.” I would respond: “If you do not know your history, you won’t know who you are!” And I heard myself say to her: “We can learn from the brilliance of the past, and one of these is the Tang.”

But what did I really mean by that? Was I trying to convince myself as much as I was trying to convince my daughter?

We spent the evening in one of the city squares, eating a half watermelon. We squatted by the flowerbeds and watched elderly couples dancing under the street lamps. The music, very kitsch 1980s Chinese songs, blasted in our ears. So at the top of my lungs I screeched at Moon about the ancient past, sounding not unlike the way the lectures were delivered in a re-education camp.

“In the beginning, Xi’an was a stone-age village. Then a long, long time ago, like 3,000 years ago, it became the centre of a kingdom. Didn’t you learn about the Trojan war in ancient Greece? So that was around the same time.”

I was already flailing, but I went on. “One of those earlier dynasties, the Zhou, was the founding dynasty of this area.” Moon started to look around, displaying her boredom. I paused, feeling a rising anguish.

“The Qin emperor – Shi Huang – decided to design his capital . It was called Xian-yang then, north-west of Xi’an. He built many palaces and unified the Chinese writing system. That was 2,000 years ago. You know he was the same one who started building the Great Wall of China .”

Moon spat out a few watermelon seeds. I searched desperately for something more dramatic.

“But he also burned a great number of books and buried the scholars alive … Can you believe that?”

“Horrible! Poor scholars!” Moon cried. “Why did he do that?”

“Well, because he wanted to control people’s thoughts. Many emperors or dictators have done similar things. Anyway, the Qin empire only lasted for a short time. Then, around 202BC , a new dynasty came, one called the Han. The first emperor was Liu Bang.”

I stopped, now frowning myself.

“What’s wrong, Mum?”

“Well, I really don’t like talking about Chinese history using western ways of counting years!”

“You mean BC or AD. I don’t like those either!”

“Yeah, what has China got to do with some man, Jesus Christ, being born so far away, who meant nothing to the emperor Liu Bang! We have our own way of dating different periods.”

Now Moon turned to look at me: “What is your Chinese way?”

I thought for a while, but I found myself fumbling. I could not translate the Chinese calendar in a simple way to an 11-year-old. The Chinese dynasty calendar is based on the name of the emperor followed by the name of the dynasty, along with a number to signify the year within that dynasty. Each new dynasty starts again from year zero.

“Just give me an example, Mum,” she said, swallowing a piece of watermelon.

“OK. We say: ‘唐高祖 12 年’, meaning the 12th year of the reign of Emperor Gaozu of the Tang. Or, in your western equivalent, AD630.”

As seemed to be so often the case, my speech to Moon was a mix of Chinese and English words. I went on, feeling like a schoolmistress. “You know, in the beginning of the Tang, in the early seventh century, Xi’an was one of the world’s largest and most populous cities.”

It is estimated that about 1 million people lived within the city walls. By the dynasty’s end, in the ninth century, the country’s population had grown from 50 million to 80 million.

For a contemporary Chinese person, numbers are essential to measure things, since we grew up in a populous country and under a governing party that was obsessed with numbers and numerical record-keeping. The Chinese Communist party would always describe a place with wording such as “the village used to have 38 Communist party members, which has expanded to 380, occupying an area of 32,000 sq metres”. We Chinese children grow up reciting numbers. Moon nodded, vaguely. Numbers are difficult for a British kid in this context.

Silent armies

Contemporary Chinese tourism is about rediscovering the country’s wondrous past, often in a banal and highly commercial fashion. History , it seems, can be a place for solace and the temporary forgetting of the stresses of contemporary Chinese life. I keenly felt that “history” was packaged as a touristic spectacle during this trip. Even so, I was confident that our travels would allow me to reassess my relationship to a past which had been entirely denied during the Cultural Revolution. I felt this intensely, and I believed that many in China felt the same way.

Once you are in Xi’an, you cannot avoid passing the site where the terracotta army was buried . The warriors are not from the Tang dynasty, but from the earlier Qin, about 2,200 years ago. After waiting in an enormously long queue outside the Qin tomb site, a great throng of tourists pushed its way into the tomb like a host of locusts. By then we were already exhausted and our water bottles were empty.

Inside the vast hall where the terracottas were displayed, the eager tourists pressed on top of one another – not unlike the statues themselves. Beneath us, on the brown earth, headless figures, broken arms and body parts were neatly laid out. Most of them bore the uniform of a Qin dynasty warrior. They were ethereally still, as though waiting, or listening, but outside of time. I felt that we ourselves had come here to be temporarily buried along with these effigies of imperial power, a living host of terracotta tourists.

These are not the traces of the Tang, though the Qin led to the Tang by way of a great tangled knot of dynastic struggle.

“If there had been no Qin dynasty, then there would be no Tang,” I said to Moon.

“So it’s like if there had been no Greeks, there would be no Romans?” she responded, boldly. She knew much more about Greek gods and Roman goddesses than I did.

I pondered what the child had said while I gazed down at the broken statues. I asserted, and she agreed, that ancient Chinese culture was as rich and advanced as ancient Greek culture. But what did it mean really? I tried to breathe better. The air inside the hall was musty and thick with dust while the army of tourists pushed us this way and that in a vortex of human interaction. At one point, my child and I were desperate to get out from under the oppressive weight of all this history .

The court diary and the sisters

Very similar to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle , or even the Domesday Book from 1,000 years ago, there is the Old Book of Tang , comprising 200 chapters that chronicle the events during the Tang era as recorded by court ministers. The book is difficult to understand as it is written in classical Chinese.

The difference between the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and the Old Book of Tang is that the former was written by monks living in monasteries, while the latter was written by mandarins living in the imperial court. Church culture was surely very different from court culture. The western church was a sanitised place peopled by men only, whereas the palace court was a luxurious and sensual inner city full of cultured courtesans and powerful women.

“It was a tradition during those times that the palace diary, or any official record, was kept by the ladies of the palace,” I said to Moon.

We had just arrived at the Huaqing hot springs, 20km from Xi’an, a site where the Tang emperors and their wives would spend their leisure time. Now it is a major tourist destination.

“But I thought women were badly treated back then, and they could not read or write,” Moon said.

“Not during the Tang! From the Tang dynasty onwards, women were celebrated for their literary and artistic skills, not just because of their beauty.”

Indeed, around the eighth century, there were five famous sisters , whose key responsibility was to keep the court diary. The sisters were the granddaughters of a well-known poet, Song Zhiwen, and were educated not only in classical poetry, but also in politics. All five became accomplished writers and thinkers, and they made a pact never to marry but to devote themselves to literature and art. Together they wrote the Analects for Women, a counterpart of the Confucian Analects from a female perspective, which became a classical text in women’s education in the Ming and Qing dynasties. In AD788, these sisters were recommended by a local official to Emperor Taizong, a great devotee of literature, who personally examined their work and recruited them all into the palace service as xueshi – masters of learning. The emperor held them in the highest esteem. It was during the Tang that, for the first time, literate women became important court ministers, called shangshu .

“That’s pretty amazing,” Moon said. “You told me that in ninth-century England, there were just Vikings raiding villages, and most people were illiterate.”

“That’s right. And if Alfred the Great had not promoted literacy, no one would be able to read except the monks.”

During the Tang, one of the areas in which women assumed an increasingly significant role was as artists, and some courtesans were famed singers and dancers, as well as being known for their extravagant clothing and hairstyles. Before the Tang, women in China were mostly veiled, and almost never in public service. The women of the Tang changed that tradition with the support of an enlightened court. They became fashion-makers, inventing elaborate makeup and sporting lavish dresses.

Would it be too pretentious, too pompous, to call the Tang era one of the earliest feminist eras in ancient history? I thought of the Anglo-Saxon women during that period, or the wives of the Vikings and Romans. I was not convinced that they had achieved such power.

The Grand Canal

In Britain, I have always lived by Regent’s Canal, around east London. After I left China, more than two decades ago, my daily routine revolved around that rusty urban English water. I would pass by the narrowboats along the winding waterways and often I thought of the Grand Canal in China . The Grand Canal is the longest and oldest artificial waterway in the world. The most ancient part was built in the fifth century BC. Later, in the seventh century AD, Emperor Yang of Sui undertook an ambitious project to connect the south and the north by a waterway. Then the Tang emperors expanded its scale and perfected its usage.

I first saw the canal in 1993 when I left my southern home town and travelled to Beijing to study. The Beijing Film Academy is located right next to the canal, by the gate of the old Yuan dynasty ruins, and a park had recently been built along the waterway, with willows hugging the banks. After the day’s classes, I would leave the campus and sit by the water, reading or eating a takeaway. The water was motionless. I always wondered how such great quantities of rice and tea had been transported on this water in olden days.

Often, on a cold sunny afternoon after snow had fallen, with one hand holding a translation of Pier Paolo Pasolini’s poetry, I would throw little stones on to the frozen surface to see if the ice would break. It was by that canal, dare I say, that I became a young intellectual, however arrogant and pretentious that may sound. I could even say that I was part of the historical landscape, stoic but everlasting, regardless of the destruction of ancient culture in China since the Cultural Revolution. For me, the Tang is the exact opposite of the Cultural Revolution. The former is rich and culturally diverse, whereas the latter is poor, unimaginative and functional in all aspects of life and thought.

When we briefly visited Beijing, I wanted to show Moon the canal and the park near the Beijing Film Academy, but I never managed to venture to that part of the capital. Beijing was too big to get around. The six massive ring roads and countless highways surrounding it seemed larger than the orbits in our solar system.

Luoyang

One might complain about the quality of water or air in China, but one can only admire the public transport: roads and railways lead to every possible destination. This is a very recent phenomenon. When I left China some 20 years ago, the infrastructure was very poor. The train from Shanghai to Beijing took two days: today it takes less than five hours.

We were on a high-speed train from Shanxi to Henan province. The landscape was lush and mountainous; the vegetation was emerald green and luminous under the sun after a rainstorm.

We arrived in Luoyang at noon, hoping the day would be cooler than the 39C we had suffered through in Xi’an.

During the Tang dynasty, Luoyang was called Dongdu (東都), the eastern capital. When Wu Zetian became empress, she constructed the tallest palace in Chinese history in Luoyang, of which there is now a duplicate in the old town, to the east of the city.

We stayed in a brand new Hyatt hotel in the new town of Luoyang. So new, in fact, that the hotel lobby was still filled with the large bundles of fresh flowers brought in for the opening celebration. From the 16th floor, I gazed down. On my left was the huge campus of the Luoyang Institute of Science and Technology; on my right was the jigsaw-like People’s Park, with sports facilities; on the horizon, skyscrapers stood in a bland, uniform line, like a monoculture forest. Where was the history? I longed for old sights and sounds.

From Luoyang, we visited the nearby Longmen Grottoes , one of the largest Buddhist sites in the world, which has survived more than 1,500 years. What a monumental sight to see countless statues of Buddha! Their elaborately sculpted details were once painted in gold. Now, all of them stood bare and colourless and most of them were missing body parts.

“Mum, do you know that there are 100,000 statues on these hills?” Moon said, reading a signpost.

“That’s a lot,” I said. “What else does it say?”

“It says there are more than 2,345 caves, some are little more than small holes, some are as large as 17 metres in height.”

As always, the Chinese fanatically list numbers when referring to any historical artefact, but anyone who visits these grottoes hardly needs to learn them. Like me, they can experience a dizzying feeling of disbelief, even as our feet stand firmly on these old rocks. Like Stonehenge in England, or the Egyptian pyramids, these monuments induce a feeling of the sublime.

As we descended toward the riverbank, I looked back at the blurred faces and figures of the Buddhist caves on the hill. How much more history could I take in one afternoon? Must we see 10,000 Buddha statues to come to the conclusion that there is a Buddha? Must we erect 20m Jesus on the cross statues to prove he died for us? Why are we so wedded to the materiality of spiritual life? Isn’t the sky vast and awesome enough to be pondered upon? Emptiness is where the richest possibility lies.

Weary and drowsy, we abandoned the sumptuous spectacle. Flagging down a taxi by the gate, we wanted to hurry back to the hotel before the rush hour, where we would deal with the small and ungodly things in our daily life, such as paying our bills, charging our phones, ordering a meal and brushing our teeth.

The Qianling Mausoleum and the

afterlife

We travelled over great distances on high-speed trains. From the northern plains we crossed over the Yangtze River and then zoomed down to southern regions, before going north again, entering the grasslands of Inner Mongolia. Moon had been tasting all sorts of strangely flavoured food and learning local dialects and could almost have passed as a native Chinese kid.

At the very end of our trip, to draw a full circle, I wanted to pay a visit to the place where the Tang emperors and empresses were buried, so we returned to Shanxi province and arrived at Qing Xian, 85km north-west from Xi’an.

Here, along the highways, even the ginkgo trees are newly planted, all trimmed, standing straight and of even height, like an obedient army waiting to be summoned to action. Even though this place was very much part of the royal centre of Chang’an during the Tang, visually there is nothing much to see now. Because of its peripheral location, its past has been totally paved over to make way for its new industrial purpose. One can see only some traces of the old ways of life half-hidden in a street corner: a tiny shoe repair place, an old tailor’s shop or a grandmother selling tea-brewed eggs by the roadside. Otherwise, large trucks carrying steel and cement rushed through streets, horns blasting.

Qianling Mausoleum is where some of the most important imperial families of the Tang dynasty are entombed. After a long, stifling ride, the bus finally dropped us in front of a large complex.

The scale of the mausoleum was something I had never seen in my life. A labyrinth to confuse anyone. Once we entered, we had to take another bus inside the vast complex, again with crowds of tourists. The bus took you up to the hills to get to the different burial sites. It was like travelling into an ancient settlement, with pavilions and waterways and inner gardens. There was even a busy street full of restaurants inside the Number Four Mausoleum site.

It was difficult to correlate the tomb numbers on the map with the actual sites. There seemed to be a lot of tombs, but few were open to the public. The sound of cicadas faded away while the noon heat was rising. Under the burning sun, we felt like two roasted ducks. We staggered towards a mausoleum that promised some air-conditioning.

We arrived at two tomb sites, one belonging to a princess and another to a prince. From the gate, we could see a sloping tunnel stretching into a darkening underground world. Cool but sepulchral air coming from the tunnel gate enticed us inside.

We followed a group of perspiring tourists, walking into the narrow tunnel. It was the tomb of Princess Yongtai . She was the seventh daughter of Emperor Zhongzong and the second daughter of his wife, Wei. She died when she was 15, apparently while giving birth.

“Oh, she died so young!” exclaimed Moon.

There were elaborate murals around us, depicting palace ladies and officials in an enchanted garden. The colours were faded and the walls full of holes and patches. As we entered further, the air became musty and heavy.

As we approached the end of the tunnel, we came upon a chamber with frescoes, and the mausoleum revealed itself. It was a miniature wooden house with carved windows and inscriptions on the surface. Inside, there was the actual coffin.

What was life like for Princess Yongtai 1,300 years ago? I could not decipher the obscure inscriptions, but what I had read earlier from the New Book of Tang told me a different story of how she died. Since the all-powerful Empress Wu was her mother-in-law, Princess Yongtai did not have an easy life. An animosity persisted between the two women. It was well known that Empress Wu led an unconventional sexual life; even in her old age, royal family members, as well as ministers, were well acquainted with her exploits. As a result, indignation and resentment accumulated in the court, and when the princess was found to be disloyal, punishment immediately ensued. According to the New Book of Tang, it was said that the princess was caned to death, though elsewhere it was recorded that she was forced to kill herself.

We did not visit the next tomb – we wanted to go straight to the most mysterious site, Empress Wu’s tomb. After much inquiry, we learned that it was impossible: no one would be allowed to enter the mausoleum of the emperor and the empress. In fact, we were told, the two main tombs were not even excavated.

So we wandered on the hills of this sacred place, sucking on our ice lollies in the shade of pine trees. We imagined a curious dark world inside the uncovered tombs, barred to modern people. Time to leave, but still we lingered on: we suspected we would never return to this place.

Along the road was a procession of statues, some headless and some armless. We walked past these ancient figures and sometimes stood before them, as if waiting for speech, a command or a bow. They stood like sturdy sentinels, without acknowledgment of our presence, their stone minds, far beyond the doings of the passing parade of tourists. I thought of John Keats’s “cold pastoral”, and felt a shiver and prickling of skin in the heat. Was that a slight puff of wind, or time itself touching our all too fragile bodies?

stories.title: The open-source AI platforms vying to become China’s Hugging Face
stories.summary: AI model platforms ModelScope and MoArk are competing to serve Chinese-speaking developers behind the Great Firewall.

stories.body:
Innovation

AI model platforms ModelScope and MoArk are competing to serve Chinese-speaking developers behind the Great Firewall.

Beijing tolerates VPN workarounds on U.S. open-source platforms like Hugging Face because total isolation would starve its domestic AI industry of global connections.

Chinese platforms like MoArk and ModelScope offer domestic open-source models to run natively on Chinese chips.

Fears that Washington could ban Chinese models from Hugging Face are accelerating the drive to build a fully sovereign tech stack.

For Beijing, managing AI requires walking a razor’s edge: seal off domestic internet users from foreign influence, but keep China’s top developers linked to the global cutting edge.

When Chinese regulators blocked U.S.-based open-source hub Hugging Face in 2023, it opened a market for domestic alternatives — even as the government quietly tolerates artificial intelligence labs bypassing the block to share Chinese models with the world.

In the AI era, China is developing an independent ecosystem faster than in the internet era.” Xu Yong, chief executive of OSChina

Alibaba i Alibaba Alibaba, founded in 1999 by Chinese entrepreneur Jack Ma, is one of the most prominent global e-commerce companies that operates platforms like AliExpress, Taobao, and Tmall. READ MORE had launched a Hugging Face-like open-model platform, ModelScope, in 2022, which now hosts more than 170,000 models. Tech company OSChina launched another open-model site, MoArk, in 2023, serving some 20,000 models.

“Not everyone is able to use a VPN [virtual private network] all the time,” Xu Yong, chief executive of OSChina, told Rest of World . Just as China’s internet industry had flourished behind the Great Firewall, the country also needed to build a self-reliant AI ecosystem to serve the Chinese-speaking population, Xu said.

“In the AI era, China is developing an independent ecosystem faster than in the internet era,” Xu said.

Unlike closed models from OpenAI and Anthropic, which are only accessible through their companies, open models can be downloaded, fine-tuned, and deployed on local hardware.

There is still this real concern in China that access to [the U.S.-based platforms] could be disrupted at any point.” Rebecca Arcesati, researcher with the think tank Mercator Institute for China Studies

New York-based Hugging Face has become the most popular place to share open models and data sets. In September, Nvidia announced it was acquiring Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, as the chipmaker bets on growing adoption of open-source models.

Beijing regulators did not disclose a specific reason when it blocked access to Hugging Face, but the Chinese government routinely blocks foreign websites that can host information it deems harmful. Chinese authorities occasionally penalized citizens for circumventing the Great Firewall without authorization. But VPN use is common in the tech industry, as developers need to access blocked sites such as Google and X in their work.

Chinese programmers have turned to global open-source platforms to share texts and images that would be censored at home. On GitHub, the Microsoft-owned platform that hosts open-source code, Chinese programmers have staged protests against long working hours and preserved news articles about Covid-19 lockdowns that had been removed from the Chinese internet.

China briefly blocked GitHub in 2013, triggering an outcry from programmers. Access was later restored. The government in 2020 endorsed Gitee, a domestic version of GitHub also owned by OSChina. But GitHub remains popular in China as the gateway to the global software community.

A wary eye on U.S. regulators

Rebecca Arcesati, a Brussels-based researcher with the think tank Mercator Institute for China Studies, said the Chinese government recognized that access to international open-source platforms was important to the development of its tech industry.

Chinese AI companies have been releasing powerful open models on Hugging Face so they can be downloaded and deployed across the world. Developers in China also need to access open models shared by people outside China.

At the same time, the government also believes that domestic platforms are more secure and reliable than those controlled by American companies and subject to U.S. regulations.

The Trump administration, which is keen on ensuring America’s lead in AI, has reportedly discussed bans on Chinese models. In a regulatory filing about the acquisition of Hugging Face, Nvidia flagged the risk that regulators could ban Chinese models from being shared on the site.

“There is still this real concern in China that access to [the U.S.-based platforms] could be disrupted at any point,” Arcesati said. “From the Chinese government’s perspective, it will be ideal if the entire technology stack for AI, including the software tools and libraries, could be indigenized as much as possible.”

“It’s our mission”

Both ModelScope and MoArk offer services similar to Hugging Face, including model testing and customization. They offer some free usage and charge users for extra computing power and advanced features.

But the number of models on the two Chinese platforms still fall far behind Hugging Face, which hosts more than 3 million open models. ModelScope said in March that it had 170,000 models and 250 million users. Xu said MoArk hosted more than 20,000 commonly used models.

To attract users, ModelScope has hosted university hackathons, where students compete to build AI applications. It also opened a coworking and event space in Hangzhou for AI entrepreneurs.

The Chinese AI industry has faced a shortage of computing power as the U.S. has banned sales of top AI chips to China. Several local companies are now racing to build advanced chips.

MoArk has deployed a team of engineers to adapt AI models to run on different types of Chinese chips, as a way to establish itself as part of China’s own AI ecosystem, according to Xu. “It’s our mission to make sure mainstream open models can run on Chinese chips,” Xu said.

AI developers in China say the main attraction of the domestic platforms is faster download speeds, though they still prefer accessing Hugging Face with a VPN. “Hugging Face and GitHub are the default in the open-source space. They offer a greater variety,” Chen Yunfei, an independent AI developer in Kunming, told Rest of World. “Domestic platforms need to convince us why we should use them.”

America is in the wrong AI race with China

The U.S. is framing its rivalry with China as one of technical superiority, failing to recognize that public trust and robust consumer protections are necessary for long-term dominance.

Dario Amodei wants to slow AI. China isn’t taking orders

Chinese officials and engineers see an attempt to preserve the U.S. lead; “Why do you always get to define the game — and change the rules?”

China is excelling in health tech. That’s good news for the world

Ruby Wang, a physician and biotech consultant in the U.K., on her upcoming book on the emergence of China as a global health superpower.

stories.summary: Aviva boss Amanda Blanc said England was "for sure" building homes that might be uninsurable at some point in the future.

Aviva boss says it 'doesn't make sense' to be building homes in flood zones as risk increases

Published 29 September 2026, 00:10 BST

Homes are being built today that could become uninsurable in the future due to the risk of flooding, the boss of insurance giant Aviva has said.

Amanda Blanc said the risk of flooding is "absolutely increasing", but based on current building patterns 115,000 new homes will be built in flood zones in the next decade.

"That doesn't seem to me to make sense. We need to think about where those homes are being built," she told the BBC.

About 6.3 million homes and businesses in England are at risk of flooding, according to the Environment Agency, and Aviva research found one in nine homes built between 2022 and 2024 are at medium to high risk of flooding.

Blanc told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast that England was "for sure" building homes that might be uninsurable at some point in the future.

"It's very well known where these flooding areas are. Let's think very carefully about homes that are being built."

Blanc said construction that borders those flood zones also needs a different approach.

"You can do all sorts of different things to your property to make it more or less vulnerable to flood," she said.

According to Aviva's research, nearly a third of new homes built in 2024 will be at risk of some flooding by 2050, and one in seven would be at medium to high risk of flooding as extreme weather becomes more acute.

Earlier this year the Met Office estimated that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters like the one experienced in the UK in 2023-24 have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events .

A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: "We've put a record amount of investment into protecting nearly 900,000 properties against billions of pounds of flooding damage.

"Meanwhile our planning proposals will help ensure that housebuilding will not go ahead in areas that are at risk of flooding, helping us to build 1.5 million homes without compromising on safety."

Homes in Loughborough were hit by floods in January last year

In a wide-ranging interview, Blanc urged the government to avoid policy "kite flying" ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget on 28 October.

Aviva is a major UK private pension provider, and Blanc said speculation over the last couple of Budgets about changes to pensions led to a significant increase in withdrawals.

"Effectively we saw in the last year 30 times the normal withdrawal from pensions that we would normally see, which is clearly something which customers may regret afterwards because once you take your tax-free lump sum out, you can't put it back in," she said.

"So we would say be very, very thoughtful about the things that you are testing, thinking about."

The few policy announcements ahead of the Budget so far have included a scheme to help first-time buyers get on to the property ladder , and a commitment from Healey to deliver a "new age of industrialisation" for the UK.

Healey has said previously that Budget speculation is unhelpful as it has a "direct impact on the decisions that investors hold back from, or may make".

A Treasury spokesperson said: "The chancellor makes tax policy decisions at fiscal events. Speculation can be harmful which is why we do not comment on future changes to tax policy."

Big Boss Interview: Aviva's Amanda Blanc

Amanda Blanc tells Sean Farrington that we are building homes that could become uninsurable in the future due to the risk of flooding - and talks about how she approaches leading a company.

Blanc said Aviva was "ready with capital" to invest in infrastructure, pointing out that the company already invests more than £100bn in the UK, £35bn of which goes into infrastructure, from hospitals to schools to windfarms.

"We've got that capital. We want to invest, we're a big UK employer. We want to invest in UK infrastructure. It provides good returns for our pension holders and for the members of those pension schemes," she said, but added detail was needed to turn it into reality.

Asked about the current debate about the pension triple lock , which means the state pension rises by the highest of either average wage increases, inflation or 2.5%, and whether the government is looking to change that, Blanc said it was not for her to say what should happen.

But potential lower annual increases to pensions if the triple lock is changed would have knock-on effects, she added.

"If you've got a lower state pension then you need a higher private pension, don't you? So you need to think about that balance," Blanc said.

stories.body:
UK mortgage approvals lowest since December 2023 as borrowing costs rise

Newsflash: the number of mortgages approved by UK lenders has fallen to its lowest level since the end of 2023.

Just 54,918 new home loans were approved in August on a seasonally-adjusted basis, new Bank of England data shows, as rising borrowing costs deterred potential home buyers.

That’s the lowest since December 2023, and some way below the average of around 60,100 over the previous 6 months.

Stripping out seasonal adjustments and there were 54,918 mortgages approved, the lowest since January (in the post-Christmas lull).

The number of approvals for remortgaging decreased to 34,000 in August, from 34,600 in July.

The BoE’s data also shows that the ‘effective’ interest rate on new mortgages increased to 4.60% in August, from 4.45% in July.

That increase was driven by rising government bond yields over the summer, as the rise in the oil price fuelled predictions of higher inflation, forcing central banks to raise interest rates.

Novo to pay $2.6bn for rights to Hengrui's weight loss drug

Back in the pharmaceuticals world, Denmark’s Novo Nordisk has secured the rights to a new weight-loss drug developed in China.

Novo will pay up to $2.6bn to Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals for the rights to its experimental weight-loss pill, called HRS-1596. The deal expands Novo’s pipeline through a second GLP-1 treatment deal with a Chinese partner.

HRS-1596 is approved in China to initiate Phase I clinical trials for weight management and type 2 diabetes.

The tie-up could help Novo to compete in the weight loss drugs market. It had emjoyed an early lead in this market with its Wegovy and Ozempic products, but rivals such as Eli Lilly have been grabbing market share with their own weight loss pills.

UK diesel prices hits new record near £2/litre

Newsflash: the price of diesel in the UK has moved closer to £2 a litre for the first time.

The average price of a litre of diesel has hit a new all-time high this morning, at 199.53p, a day after hitting a new record high of 199.18p.

Since the Iran war began, the average price of diesel has risen by 40%, as the jump in crude oil prices drove up the cost of refined products too.

Attacks on Russia’s oil refinery by Ukraine have also pushed up diesel prices, prompting warnings that motorists and businesses are facing painfully higher prices at the pumps.

Motor fuel prices across Europe have hit record levels in recent weeks, prompting calls for political leaders to take action to safeguard consumers against rising cost pressures.

Biz secretary battling for more energy cost support

Business secretary Jonathan Reynolds has suggested he’s fighting for more support for businesses with their energy costs, ahead of next month’s budget.

Asked about soaring costs in a fringe meeting at Labour conference this morning, Reynolds said:

double quotation mark “I go to bed thinking about industrial energy prices, and I wake up thinking about it.”

He highlighted the existing British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme which will cut costs for some firms - but hinted he would like to do more, saying:

double quotation mark “It’s one of the strongest causes I fight in government and I have done from day one and I continue to do that - and I think my arguments are strong.”

O2 Business CEO is leaving

Jo Bertram, the chief executive of mobile giant O2’s business operation, is leaving the company after eight years, my colleagues Anna Isaac and Mark Sweney report.

Bertram , a former senior Uber executive who also sits on the board of Sainsbury’s, will be replaced on an interim basis by Matt Riley, the chair of O2 Business .

Bertram joined the telecoms company in 2018 after abruptly leaving Uber after the ride hailing service battled regulators which at the time had banned it from operating in London.

Her departure comes after seeing through the initial phase of the combination of O2 Business and telecoms group Daisy Group , which merged last year to create a £3bn business telecoms group with hundreds of thousands of customers including Sainsbury’s, the NHS and British Sugar.

In April the operation, initially branded as O2 Daisy with Virgin Media O2 holding a 70% stake, was rebranded as O2 Business.

Bertram was originally hired by Telefonica in March 2018 as chief digital and strategy officer of O2.

Two years later Virgin Media, then 100% owned by US cable giant Liberty Global, and Telefonica announced a £31bn mega merger of their UK operations.

Earlier this month the business, which is jointly owned by Liberty Global and Telefonica, reportedly kicked off a £600m cost-cutting programme including job cuts as it looks to deal with a £22bn debt pile.

A spokesman for VMO2 confirmed Bertram’s departure, saying:

double quotation mark “Jo has held a number of executive positions during her time within the company and played a pivotal role in the completion of the merger between O2 Business and Daisy Group, successfully leading integration activity during the first year of the new business. We’d like to thank Jo for her leadership and significant contribution during her time at the company.”

UK mortgage rates are unlikely to drop back unless energy prices fall, warns Simon Gammon , managing partner at Knight Frank Finance :

double quotation mark “Buying activity weakened through the summer as rising energy prices pushed up borrowing costs. Lending to homebuyers fell 15% in August compared to the same month a year earlier. At the time, leading fixed rates were edging closer to 4.5% – they’ve since risen to 4.8%. “The large lenders are doing business with very thin margins in an attempt to retain market share, which leaves them vulnerable to swap rate volatility. Without a sustained fall in energy prices, leading fixed rates are likely to remain around 4.5% through the autumn selling season, which will keep a lid on activity. “The government’s announcement of a first-time buyer support scheme will provide a boost to sentiment, particularly in more affordable parts of the country, but mortgage rates remain the bigger constraint. A meaningful recovery in transaction volumes is likely to require a sustained improvement in borrowing costs.”

UK pays highest yield since 1999 at 10-year bond auction

Newsflash: Britain’s government has paid the highest interest rate since 1999 on a sale of 10-year bonds.

An £4.25bn auction of a new UK gilt maturing in 2036 has just concluded, with bond investors successfully demanding an average yield of 5.383% when bidding to buy the debt.

That’s the highest yield, or interest rate, since September 1999, Reuters reports.

The auction, held by the Debt Management Office , received bids for more than three times as much debt as was for sale, showing investors were still keen to buy UK debt, but at a price….

This results follows months of turmoil in the government bond markets, driven by inflation fears, which has driven up the yield on debt traded between bond investors.

Today’s auction highlights that those moves have real implications for the government, as higher bond yields push up the cost of servicing the national debt.

Earlier this month, the UK government was forced to pay the highest interest rate for a 30-year bond since 1998 .

The fall in mortgage approvals last month shows that higher borrowing costs are taking a toll on activity in the housing sector, reports Paul Dales , chief UK economist at Capital Economics .

Dales told clients:

double quotation mark Even though the Bank of England has not (yet) raised interest rates, the further fall in mortgage approvals from 56,000 in July to 54,900 in August (the lowest since December 2023) shows that the sharp rise in mortgage rates is restraining activity. At face, value, that’s consistent with house price inflation slowing from 1.7% in August to around 0% in six months’ time.

Higher borrowing costs and continued macroeconomic uncertainty are “slamming the brakes on the mortgage market”, warns Richard Pinch, senior director at banking and credit advisory consultancy Broadstone .

Responding to this morning’s data showing a drop in mortgage approvals , Pinch says:

double quotation mark “Despite some of the green shoots of economic recovery we have seen through the year, affordability pressures are clearly still biting as households head towards another challenging winter. “The sharp rise in consumer credit borrowing, particularly on credit cards, suggests more households are leaning on credit to absorb everyday cost pressures. “For lenders, the priority must be to identify signs of financial strain as early as possible and ensure borrowers have access to appropriate support and flexibility before temporary affordability pressures become more serious.”

UK mortgage rates up again

UK mortgage rates have nudged higher this morning, Moneyfacts reports.

They say:

The average 2-year fixed residential mortgage rate today is 5.93%. This is up from 5.91% the previous working day.

The average 5-year fixed residential mortgage rate today is 5.94%. This is up from 5.93% the previous working day.

This lifts the average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate to the highest since 10 July 2024, while the average five-year rate has returned to its highest since 10 October 2023.

UK metal flow engineering firm Vesuvius could soon be the latest British company to fall to an overseas takeover.

London-based Vesuvius has just told the City that it has received “a series of” unsolicited takeover approaches from Austria’s RHI Magnesita over the last year.

The most recent values Vesuvius’s share at 551p each, a large premium on last night’s closing price of 374p.

The company says:

double quotation mark The Board of Vesuvius is evaluating the Latest Proposal carefully, including the financial terms and execution risk associated with the proposed transaction, together with its financial and legal advisers, and a further announcement will be made as appropriate.

This morning, Vesuvius’s shares have jumped almost 25% to 464p.

UK government bond prices are rising as the City waits to hear from prime minister Andy Burnham later today.

Burnham is due to address the Labour party conference at 2pm, and there are reports that the prime minister could signal the end of the pensions triple lock, by suggesting it should be reviewed in the party’s next manifesto.

This could help to fund a new social care system, which Labour insiders hope to sell to the public before the next election.

Last weekend, the PM told the Guardian that it was “crucial” to have fiscal stability – remarks which could reassure investors that it won’t embark on a reckless borrowing splurge.

This morning, the yield on 10-year UK bonds is down 4.4 basis points (0.044 of a percentage point) at 5.385%. Thirty-year gilt yields are down 4bps at 5.878%, both below the multi-year highs set this month.

Shorter-dated borrowing costs are down too, with two-year bond yields down 4.6bps to 4.886%.

AstraZeneca hits two-month high after Summit deal

Shares in AstraZeneca have jumped by 2% at the start of stock market trading in London, hitting a two-month high.

That puts them among the top risers on the London Stock Exchange, along with a group of mining companies including Antofagasta (+1.9%) and Anglo American (+1.75%)

And in a FURTHER reminder of those dangers…. OpenAI has apologised to Australians for hacking a government website this summer

In a blog post released on Tuesday, OpenAI said it should have handled its response to the attack on Medicare better, saying:

double quotation mark “In June, during internal training and evaluation our models accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not authorised to. We also should have handled our response better. We are sorry and working to do better in the future.”

OpenAI scraps release of new model over safety concerns in internal testing

In another example of the risks of AI, OpenAI is scrapping the release of GPT-6.1 Astra, a next-generation ⁠model planned for an October debut, over safety concerns raised by researchers ⁠during internal testing.

The ⁠ Wall ​Street Journal reported on Monday that the model, expected to appear in ChatGPT and ⁠Codex, was designed to handle more complex tasks without human assistance.

However, it has failed OpenAI’s ‘alignment tests’, which assess whether a ​system follows human intent:

The model showed more deception than its predecessor, including at times failing to accurately disclose actions it had or had not taken.

It also had problems with “scope authorization”, pushing ahead with ​tasks ​without requesting user permission ​and sometimes attempting to use external tools ​or services ‌when doing so could ​be ​unsafe.

The Financial Times have also scrutinised Anthropic’s IPO prospectus, and report that the Claude maker also provided investors with a clearer picture of the challenging economics of building state of the art AI models.

The FT says :

double quotation mark Anthropic said it plans to spend $518bn on cloud, computing and infrastructure obligations in the coming years to support its rapid growth. The AI lab’s backers are confident Anthropic can list at a valuation of over $2tn, more than double the level achieved in its last funding round in May and beyond the $1.78tn achieved by Elon Musk’s SpaceX in June. They point to its extraordinary growth rate to justify their bullishness.

AstraZeneca invests $2bn in Summit in cancer drug tie-up

Pharmaceuticals news: AstraZeneca is investing $2bn in biopharmaceutical oncology company Summit Therapeutics, as part of a tie-up to jointly develop and test anti-cancer drugs.

Announcing the deal, AstraZeneca says the two companies will collaborate on a ‌series of studies testing their cancer treatments together.

They hope to accelerate the development of ivonescimab , a next-generation cancer treatment licensed by Summit which stops tumor growth and help the body’s immune system attack cancer.

Ivonescimab works by simultaneously blocking PD-1, which helps cancer evade the immune system, and VEGF, which tumors use to grow blood vessels, helping the immune system better find and attack cancer cells.

Susan Galbraith , executive vice president for oncology haematology R&D at AstraZeneca , explains:

double quotation mark “A core pillar of our oncology strategy is to broaden the reach of our ADC portfolio as the backbone of treatment across tumour types with combinations alongside next-generation immunotherapies. Bispecifics targeting PD-1 and VEGF are rapidly advancing in development and have the potential to improve on current immunotherapies, particularly in lung, breast and gastrointestinal cancers. This opportunity to combine ivonescimab with AstraZeneca’s ADC portfolio, including with Sone-Ve, could enable new regimens that raise the bar for patients with cancer across the treatment landscape.”

Under the deal, AstraZeneca is paying $2bn to receive 12% of Summit’s shares.

Introduction: Anthropic warns AI may pose 'existential risks to humanity' in IPO filing

Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

Anthropic’s plan to float on the stock market has provided a sobering insight into the risks that AI poses, even as it attempts to pull off a massive share sale to the public.

Reuters has taken a look at Anthropic’s IPO prospectus – the legal document that outlines a company’s financial details before it floats on the stock market – and found that it includes a warning that advanced AI could be a “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

The filing explains:

double quotation mark “Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm.”

And following a flurry of stories about AI models going rogue, Anthropic flags that its models could conceal information and exhibit behavior resembling blackmail, and resist efforts to shut them down.

It cautions:

double quotation mark “Potential model awareness of our evaluation efforts creates a significant limitation on our ability to assess model safety.”

Such warnings appear across 80 pages (!) devoted to risk factors in the prospectus, almost a third of the document.

Despite these warnings, Anthropic – which created the Claude chatbot – is aiming for one of the largest stock market flotations ever, which could value it at more than $2tn.

The IPO prospectus shows that Anthropic’s revenue grew 12-fold in 2025 to nearly $4.6bn – with nearly a quarter coming from just two customers.

But… its operating loss swelled to over $8bn last year, from nearly $3bn in 2024.

The IPO is expected to take place after the US midterm elections in November, and will be a serious test of investor interest, and concern, around AI.

Yesterday, a group of senior AI executives – and two of the “godfathers” of the technology – warned governments to prepare for an AI “intelligence explosion”.

stories.title: Chris Mason: Burnham opens debate on huge issue of social care reform
stories.summary: The pitch from Andy Burnham is that there needs to be a willingness to say "the things politicians usually avoid", the BBC's political editor writes.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 29 September 2026, 11:15 BST

Conference speech day is always a big day for a prime minister, and perhaps no bigger than when it is your first one in the role.

The pitch from Burnham is that "hope comes from honesty," there needs to be "less drift and more direction" and there needs to be a willingness to say "the things politicians usually avoid."

On Sunday, he told the BBC he wants to shake up social care in England , but would only be able to do so after a general election given he was committed to the tax promises Sir Keir Starmer made at the last general election.

This prompted a flurry of chat about how his social care plan could be paid for - and in particular the future of what is known as the triple lock, the promise to increase the state pension in line with wages, prices or 2.5%, whichever is the highest.

This was a policy introduced in 2010 by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government to try to address pensioner poverty.

But plenty of politicians, in multiple parties, have long privately fretted that its cost is ballooning and will continue to do so, but would bemoan how politically difficult it would be to drop it.

It's a tricky one for the prime minister: he has the leader of the Unite union, Sharon Graham, saying it could be "electoral suicide" to ditch the triple lock.

Meanwhile the markets - which determine the cost of borrowing for the government - are keeping a keen eye on whether Burnham's promises appear to be financially credible.

In other words, he has to be able to point to things where money won't be spent, as well as where it will be.

No10 are being pretty coy about precisely what Andy Burnham will or won't say on all this later on.

They really don't want to overcook it or overdo it, instead suggesting it is others who have been getting carried away.

But ministers are well aware that a hare is running about it all - and given that, it would be extraordinary if there was no mention of it all, given that promise about "honesty," candour and trade offs.

Sufficiently extraordinary that his critics would pounce on what they'd see as a precise lack of the very thing he is promising - candour.

Why the PM could finally drop the triple lock pension pledge Published 1 day ago

Burnham to unveil public body to invest in electricity grid Published 3 hours ago

Folk I am hearing from this morning suggest, as one figure put it, "people will be surprised on the upside" about how much Burnham will be willing to lean into the options that could be explored as part of Labour's offer at the next general election.

He will be explicit it will be retained, as promised, until the election.

Instead, it would appear Burnham will seek to seed a conversation about all of the above, without nailing down the details.

His allies see this as a different approach to politics – being open about options, starting a debate but not crudely or abruptly shifting policy.

There is an implicit comparison with Sir Keir Starmer's ditching of the Winter Fuel Payment – which appeared to come from nowhere and had a near immediate impact.

But that didn't stop Graham likening the two approaches – claiming "the danger of doing it" is that Labour could "waste" a second hearing which it now has under Andy Burnham.

And so the debate begins.

In the round, though, ministers I speak to are relishing what they see as a return to big arguments, about generational issues with a prime minister willing to wrestle with them in public.

This afternoon we will get a fuller sense of the scope and scale of that – on social care, pensions and much else.
